data.title: Middle East Eye: Why is Turkey warning of an Israeli military operation in Syria?
data.author: Mera Aladam
data.summary:
Why is Turkey warning of an Israeli military operation in Syria?
Turkey's foreign minister has warned that Israel could launch a military operation in Syria, accusing it of backing a faction within the country's Druze community in an attempt to provoke the Syrian army and create a pretext for intervention.
Hakan Fidan made the remarks in a televised interview with Turkish broadcaster TGRT Haber on Saturday, saying Ankara had raised the possibility with regional allies, as well as US and European officials.
"There is a scenario in which the Israeli army uses this as a pretext to launch an operation against Syria," Fidan said.
The Turkish foreign minister also alleged that Israel was supporting one of three major factions within Syria's Druze community, supplying it with weapons and ammunition by helicopter on a weekly basis.

data.title: Middle East Eye: From arson to land seizures: Settlers tighten grip on Palestinian villages near Ramallah
data.author: Mera Aladam
data.summary:
From arson to land seizures: Settlers tighten grip on Palestinian villages near Ramallah
In a series of coordinated attacks across several villages near the city of Ramallah in the central occupied West Bank, Israeli settlers torched Palestinian vehicles between Saturday evening and Sunday morning.
The settlers also spray-painted racist slogans on the walls of homes in the three villages, calling for the killing of Arabs and for revenge against them.
Rafat Abu Musa, head of the village council of Deir al-Sudan, north of Ramallah, told Middle East Eye that settlers infiltrated the southern part of the village at 11.30pm on Saturday and set fire to two vehicles.
They spray-painted slogans in Hebrew on the walls of nearby houses, he said, adding that the same area had been targeted by a similar attack two months ago, during which a vehicle was set on fire.
Abu Musa indicated that the settlers came from a newly built outpost on the summit of Jabal al-Ras, located in the neighbouring village of Umm Safa.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Netanyahu, Eisenkot parties end talks without deal on forming government
data.author: Ayse Betul Aytekin
data.summary:
Netanyahu, Eisenkot parties end talks without deal on forming government
The parties of caretaker Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his rival Gadi Eisenkot concluded a new round of talks on Sunday without reaching an agreement on a possible coalition government, which would require concessions from both sides.
Delegations from Eisenkot’s Yashar party and Netanyahu’s Likud met for four hours at a hotel in Herzliya, near Tel Aviv, following a first round of discussions last Sunday.
“The latest round of coalition talks… has concluded. The two sides outlined their positions on a range of substantive issues and discussed them in detail,” the two parties said in a joint statement.
“A follow-up meeting will be held,” they added, without specifying a date or revealing any other details.
A former army chief of staff, Eisenkot has until 6 December to form a government, with the possibility of a 14‑day extension, after October elections failed to give either camp an absolute majority.
His 48-member bloc, which needs 61 lawmakers to reach a majority, remains divided over whether to build a coalition through an alliance with ultra‑Orthodox parties, a rapprochement with Arab parties, or a national unity government with Likud.
Netanyahu is pushing for a national unity government, which could see a rotation of the premiership between the two men.
Pedestrians walk past an advertisement featuring Benjamin Netanyahu (R) of the Likud party and leader of the Yashar party Gadi Eisenkot, along a street in Ramat Gan on 23 September 2026 (AFP)

data.title: Middle East Eye: Workers shot, villagers trapped: Israeli forces and settlers attack Palestinian towns across West Bank
data.author: Ayse Betul Aytekin
data.summary:
Workers shot, villagers trapped: Israeli forces and settlers attack Palestinian towns across West Bank
Israeli forces and settlers carried out raids and attacks across the occupied West Bank on Sunday, injuring and detaining Palestinians, the Palestinian news agency Wafa reported. The attacks come amid a sharp escalation in settler violence in the territory.
Overnight into Sunday, Israeli settlers attacked three Palestinian villages, setting fire to 12 vehicles and spray-painting racist slogans on residential buildings.
The attacks targeted Kafr Malik, Deir Abu Mash'al and Deir al-Sudan, in the Ramallah and al-Bireh governorate.
Near Hizma, north-east of Jerusalem, Israeli forces fired live ammunition at Palestinian workers trying to cross the separation wall into the city, wounding several of them, according to the Jerusalem Governorate.
Around 18 workers were detained, and video footage showed one of them being severely beaten.
The Palestine Red Crescent said it treated two people who were injured after being beaten by Israeli forces and falling from the wall. Israeli forces later closed the entrances to Hizma and forced shops to shut.
In al-Mughayyir, north-east of Ramallah, several Palestinians were injured by flying glass when settlers attacked vehicles on Sunday evening, the head of the village council, Amin Abu Alia, told Wafa.
Abu Alia said settlers, protected by Israeli forces, gathered at the village entrances and prevented residents from entering or leaving. He added that Israeli forces detained several Palestinians, and that there was no information so far on their fate or whereabouts.
Many Palestinian residents were also left stranded in the neighbouring village of Abu Falah, unable to return home.
South of Jenin, Israeli forces raided the towns of Anza, Jaba', Arraba and Ya'bad. Video footage showed Palestinian man severely beaten by Israeli soldiers inside his house in Ya'bad.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Eisenkot condemns 'Jewish terrorism' near Ramallah as US congressman calls for accountability
data.author: Ayse Betul Aytekin
data.summary:
Eisenkot condemns 'Jewish terrorism' near Ramallah as US congressman calls for accountability
Israeli opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot has condemned a series of arson attacks by settlers in the occupied West Bank as "Jewish terrorism", accusing far-right ministers Bezalel Smotrich and Itamar Ben Gvir of fuelling violence against Palestinians.
Overnight into Sunday, Israeli settlers attacked three Palestinian villages near Ramallah, setting fire to vehicles and spray-painting racist slogans on residential buildings.
Eisenkot, leader of the Yashar party, described the attacks as "Jewish terrorism in every sense of the word" and called on the government and security establishment to take tougher action against violent settlers.
"The acts of sabotage carried out by extremist groups setting fire to vehicles and homes undermine regional stability, endanger lives and seriously harm Israel's national security and foreign relations," he wrote on X.
Politician Yair Lapid also condemned the attacks, calling them "Jewish terrorism" caused by government negligence.
"Jewish terrorism is the product of criminal negligence on the part of the Israeli government," Lapid said. "By remaining silent, government ministers are deliberately encouraging these pogroms."
"When we form a government, we will tackle this terrorism and restore governance, law and order," he added.
In the United States, Democratic Congressman Josh Gottheimer condemned the attacks and called for accountability.
"These incidents warrant a full and thorough investigation," Gottheimer wrote on X, adding that vigilante justice had "no place" in society.
Israeli police said they had opened investigations into arson, vandalism and property damage.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Israel carries out more demolitions in southern Lebanon
data.author: Ayse Betul Aytekin
data.summary:
Israel carries out more demolitions in southern Lebanon
Israeli forces detonated explosives to destroy structures on the outskirts of Qantara in southern Lebanon, Lebanon's National News Agency (NNA) reported.
Earlier on Sunday, Israeli forces set off a massive explosion in Zawtar al-Sharqiyah, followed by another in Kfar Tibnit, according to NNA.
The blasts could be heard across much of southern Lebanon.
Residents of Nabatieh al-Fawqa and Zawtar held two separate protests against the Lebanese government's "silence" over Israel's occupation of areas up to the Litani River, which began in March, according to NNA.
Parliament Speaker Nabih Berri said he would not accept congratulations on Lebanon's Independence Day, which falls on 22 November, in solidarity with residents of the occupied southern border villages.
In a statement, Berri described this year's independence as "incomplete and unfulfilled".
He said it would be complete only once Lebanese territory was liberated and official and popular positions were united again.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Watch: Palestinians describe fear after Israeli settlers attack West Bank villages
data.author: Mera Aladam
data.summary:
Watch: Palestinians describe fear after Israeli settlers attack West Bank villages
Palestinian residents in the occupied West Bank have described how Israeli settlers set fire to vehicles and sprayed racist graffiti on homes during overnight attacks on several villages.
Footage from Deir Abu Mashal and Kafr Malik on Sunday shows burnt-out cars and graffiti reading "Death to Arabs" and "Revenge" painted on walls. Residents said settlers attacked their villages while families were asleep, leaving multiple vehicles destroyed.
"We were sleeping and not expecting that herds of settlers will attack our homes while people are sleeping, we never expected this," said Muneer Alkhatib, a resident of Deir Abu Mashal.
Another resident, Montaser Almalki, said the attackers came from a nearby settler outpost and warned that his family could have been caught in a fire had they not woken up.
The attacks took place across several locations in the occupied West Bank. They were condemned by Israeli opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot, who described them as "Jewish terrorism" and blamed far-right ministers Itamar Ben Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich for encouraging the violence.

Trump claims he predicted drops in oil prices, stock market and hits from Iran after Democratic win in midterm elections
US President Donald Trump claimed that he predicted a stock market decline as well as harsher attacks from Iran after the Democratic Party's victory in the recent midterm elections.
"As everyone remembers, I predicted two things concerning the November 3rd Midterm Elections. One, that if the Democrats win, the Stock Markets would go down, substantially, which they have, and two, that the Islamic Republic of Iran... will grow more aggressive in their attacks, which has also occurred," he wrote in a post on his social media platform Truth Social.
Trump added that Iran "launched more drones and missiles in the last week than at any time for over a year", but claimed that the attacks have "all been knocked down, and done no damage".
"Iranian leaders consider the Democrats weak, ineffective, and Country destroying, but I won’t let that happen! Both the Dems and Iran fought like hell to keep the Oil price up as long as possible and, since the Election, the Oil price has dropped by a record level," the American president further claimed.
Trump went onto describe the elections as "very strange".

data.title: Middle East Eye: Opinion: Anti-Muslim racism is a global system used to normalise mass killing
data.author: Mera Aladam
data.summary:
Opinion: Anti-Muslim racism is a global system used to normalise mass killing
Dr Amina Shareef, a researcher of anti-Muslim racism, says that the destruction unfolding in Gaza, Iran and Lebanon is part of a longer history of anti-Muslim racism that has made mass Muslim suffering and death politically permissible.
She says that Islamophobia is not simply a matter of prejudice or discrimination, but a global system of racial power that constructs Muslims and those identified as Muslim as security threats, allowing violence against them to be justified in the name of security.
Central to this system is the figure of the Muslim terrorist, which portrays Muslim political agency as inherently threatening. Shareef says that this logic extends beyond surveillance, detention and militarised borders to warfare, political abandonment and the destruction of the conditions necessary for life.
She identifies Palestine as a key site where contemporary security practices and technologies of control have been refined and reproduced elsewhere, a process she describes through the concept of the “Palestine boomerang”. Although conflicts in Iran, Lebanon, Kashmir, Syria, Yemen, Iraq and Afghanistan have distinct histories, she argues that they reveal a recurring pattern in which Muslim populations are portrayed as threats and their suffering becomes easier to justify.
Shareef concludes that confronting anti-Muslim racism is ultimately a struggle to protect life and human dignity. She calls for sustained resistance to systems that expose entire populations to premature death, arguing that the responsibility to seek justice remains even when the outcome is uncertain.

Ukraine has claimed responsibility for sinking a Russian warship at a naval base in eastern Libya, in a major expansion of its maritime campaign against Moscow that has brought the nearly five-year war into the Mediterranean.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said Ukrainian forces deployed seven domestically made naval drones to attack the Russian corvette Merkury at Benghazi Naval Base on Sunday.
The attack, which took place about 2,400km from Ukraine's front line, was among Kyiv's most far-reaching operations against Russian naval assets since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022.
“Despite all the enemy's efforts to counter the attack, the Russian corvette Merkury was sunk,” Zelensky said in a post on X on Monday.
“We continue our operations in designated waters. We are responding to Russia's aggression. We are developing Ukrainian weapons,” he added.
Ukraine's internal security agency, known as the SBU, described the operation as “unique”, saying the Merkury regularly escorted Russian naval convoys, including the dry cargo ship MV Angara, which it accused Moscow of using to transport military equipment.
The SBU said the naval drones were launched from a “mothership” near the target and that Russian forces attempted to intercept them using air, sea and land defences.

The message was quick and abrupt. It was texted to me by my dear friend, the pre-eminent Palestinian filmmaker Mai Masri. I have known Mai and followed her extraordinary work closely for decades.
The last time I had seen Masri in person was when we hosted her at Columbia University for the screening of her latest documentary, Beirut: Eye of the Storm (2021). Before that, we had also hosted the New York premiere of her 3000 Nights (2015).
On our campus, as on many others, Mai Masri's name is held in the highest respect, love and admiration.
Her legendary documentaries, like Under the Rubble (1983), Wild Flowers: Women of South Lebanon (1986), War Generation (1989) and Children of Fire (1990), have consolidated her significance as one of the most gifted, principled and iconic Palestinian filmmakers of her generation.
